questions.question:
Triangle DEF is inscribed in a semicircle of radius t, with DF the flat edge of the semicircle and E on the curved edge. DE = a and EF = b.
Column A: a^2 + b^2
Column B: 4t^2
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M65 175 A95 95 0 0 1 255 175" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="65" y1="175" x2="255" y2="175" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="65" y1="175" x2="200" y2="89" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="89" x2="255" y2="175" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="192,94 197,103 205,97" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="160" cy="175" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="152" y="196" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">O</text><text x="50" y="192" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">D</text><text x="200" y="78" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">E</text><text x="258" y="192" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">F</text><text x="116" y="126" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">a</text><text x="240" y="126" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">b</text><text x="204" y="192" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">t</text></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: The flat edge DF of a semicircle is a diameter, so DF = 2t. Because E lies on the curved edge, angle DEF is inscribed in a semicircle and is therefore a right angle, with DF as the hypotenuse of right triangle DEF. The Pythagorean theorem then gives a^2 + b^2 = DF^2 = (2t)^2 = 4t^2. The two quantities are equal wherever E sits on the arc.
questions.trap: Students take DF to be t rather than 2t and compare a^2 + b^2 with t^2, concluding that Column A is greater. The radius is t, so the diameter that serves as the hypotenuse is twice that, and squaring it brings in the factor of 4.

questions.question:
Two distinct line segments of equal length bisect each other.
Column A: the number of distinct circles that pass through at least three of the four endpoints
Column B: 3
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: When two segments bisect each other, their four endpoints form a parallelogram, and when the two segments are also equal in length, that parallelogram has equal diagonals, which makes it a rectangle. The four vertices of a rectangle are concyclic: the circle centered at the common midpoint, with radius equal to half a diagonal, passes through all four. Any three of the four points determine exactly one circle, and since all four already lie on a single circle, every such choice produces that same circle. So Column A equals 1, which is less than 3.
questions.trap: Students count the four ways of choosing three endpoints out of four and answer 4, making Column A the larger quantity. Three points do determine a unique circle, but here all four choices land on the very same circle, so the four selections give one circle, not four.

questions.question:
In the circle with center O and radius k, A and B are points on the circle and AB is not a diameter.
Column A: the perimeter of triangle AOB
Column B: 3.5k

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="160" cy="120" r="88" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="160" y1="120" x2="77" y2="90" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="160" y1="120" x2="217" y2="53" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="77" y1="90" x2="217" y2="53" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="160" cy="120" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="154" y="138" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">O</text><text x="58" y="86" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">A</text><text x="223" y="46" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">B</text><text x="112" y="118" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">k</text><text x="192" y="100" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">k</text></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Two sides of triangle AOB are radii, so OA = OB = k and the perimeter is 2k + AB. The chord AB can be made as short as we like by bringing A and B close together, and it can be pushed up toward but never reaching the diameter 2k, so AB ranges over everything strictly between 0 and 2k. The perimeter therefore ranges over everything strictly between 2k and 4k, and 3.5k lies inside that interval. Depending on where A and B sit, the perimeter can be less than, equal to, or greater than 3.5k.
questions.trap: Students picture a roughly symmetric chord, estimate AB at about 1.5k, get a perimeter near 3.5k, and choose C. Nothing in the problem pins down the central angle, so the chord length is free and the comparison stays open.

questions.question: Equilateral triangle PQR is inscribed in a circle whose area is 36*pi. What is the length of an altitude of triangle PQR?
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="160" cy="120" r="85" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="160" y1="35" x2="86" y2="163" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="86" y1="163" x2="234" y2="163" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="234" y1="163" x2="160" y2="35" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="160" y1="35" x2="160" y2="163" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polyline points="148,163 148,151 160,151" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="160" cy="120" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="166" y="116" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">O</text><text x="154" y="26" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">P</text><text x="68" y="176" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">Q</text><text x="240" y="176" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">R</text></svg>
questions.explanation: From area 36*pi we get pi*r^2 = 36*pi, so the radius is 6. For an equilateral triangle the center of the circumscribed circle is also the centroid, and the centroid divides each altitude in a 2 to 1 ratio measured from the vertex. The longer piece is the circumradius, so 6 is two thirds of the altitude. That makes the altitude 6 x (3/2) = 9.
questions.trap: Students take the altitude to be the diameter, 12, imagining it stretching from the top of the circle to the bottom. The altitude ends at the midpoint of the opposite side, which is inside the circle, not at the circle itself, so it falls short of the diameter by the one-third piece below the center.

questions.question: In the figure, O is the center of the circle of radius 3, and OPQR is a parallelogram with OP and OR both radii of the circle. The measure of angle POR is 60 degrees. What is the area of the shaded region, the part of the parallelogram that lies outside the circle?
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M114 102 L156 60 L172 118 A60 60 0 0 0 114 102 Z" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"/><circle cx="130" cy="160" r="60" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="130" y1="160" x2="114" y2="102" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="130" y1="160" x2="172" y2="118" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="114" y1="102" x2="156" y2="60" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="172" y1="118" x2="156" y2="60" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M123.1 134.9 A26 26 0 0 1 148.4 141.6" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="130" cy="160" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="112" y="178" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">O</text><text x="94" y="98" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">P</text><text x="160" y="52" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">Q</text><text x="178" y="116" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">R</text><text x="104" y="134" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">3</text><text x="156" y="148" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">3</text><text x="143" y="125" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937" text-anchor="middle">60°</text></svg>
questions.explanation: The part of the parallelogram inside the circle is exactly the sector cut off by radii OP and OR, since every point of the parallelogram lies within the 60 degree wedge. That sector is 60/360 = 1/6 of the circle, so its area is (1/6)(pi)(3^2) = 3*pi/2. The parallelogram itself has two adjacent sides of length 3 with a 60 degree angle between them, so its area is 3 x 3 x sin(60) = 9*sqrt(3)/2. Subtracting, the shaded area is 9*sqrt(3)/2 - 3*pi/2.
questions.trap: Students treat the parallelogram as a rectangle and use 3 x 3 = 9 for its area, which gives 9 - 3*pi/2, about 4.29 — a plausible-looking number that is simply wrong. The 60 degree angle means the height is 3*sin(60), not 3, so the sine factor cannot be dropped.

questions.question: The shaded region shown is what remains of a rectangle 3r units wide and 2r units tall after a quarter circle of radius r is removed at each of the four corners, each quarter circle having its center at that corner. What is the perimeter of the shaded region?
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M100 160 L160 160 A60 60 0 0 1 220 100 A60 60 0 0 1 160 40 L100 40 A60 60 0 0 1 40 100 A60 60 0 0 1 100 160 Z" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="40" y1="180" x2="220" y2="180" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="40" y1="175" x2="40" y2="185" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="220" y1="175" x2="220" y2="185" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="245" y1="40" x2="245" y2="160" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="240" y1="40" x2="250" y2="40" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="240" y1="160" x2="250" y2="160" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="122" y="199" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">3r</text><text x="256" y="105" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">2r</text></svg>
questions.explanation: Walk the boundary. Along the bottom edge, the two corner cuts each swallow r of the 3r width, leaving a straight piece of length r; the same happens along the top, for another r. Along each vertical edge of height 2r, the two cuts swallow r each and meet exactly in the middle, so no straight piece survives there at all. That accounts for 2r of straight boundary. In place of the eight straight pieces removed, the boundary now runs along four quarter circles of radius r, whose total length is 4 x (1/4)(2*pi*r) = 2*pi*r. The perimeter is therefore (2 + 2*pi)r.
questions.trap: Students take the rectangle's perimeter of 10r and add the four arcs to it, answering (10 + 2*pi)r. Each arc replaces two straight pieces of length r rather than being tacked on, so 8r has to come off before the arcs go on.

questions.question: A certain alloy has a mass of 4 grams per cubic centimeter. A bar of this alloy in the shape of a rectangular solid has a mass of 1,000 grams. The bar is 5 centimeters wide and is twice as long as it is high. How many centimeters high is the bar?
questions.explanation: Mass divided by density gives volume, so the bar occupies 1,000/4 = 250 cubic centimeters. Let the height be h; then the length is 2h and the width is 5, so the volume is 5 x h x 2h = 10*h^2. Setting 10*h^2 = 250 gives h^2 = 25 and h = 5.
questions.trap: Students divide the volume by the width alone, getting 250/5 = 50, and choose that as the height. That quotient is the product of the length and the height, not the height itself, and it still has to be split between two dimensions that are in a 2 to 1 ratio.

questions.question: Two right circular cylindrical containers stand upright. The larger has an inside radius of 5 inches and the smaller an inside radius of 2 inches, and each has an inside height of 15 inches. The smaller container is filled with water to a depth of 10 inches, and all of that water is then poured into the empty larger container. What is the depth of the water, in inches, in the larger container?
questions.explanation: The water in the smaller container forms a cylinder of radius 2 and height 10, so its volume is pi(2^2)(10) = 40*pi cubic inches. Poured into the larger container, that same volume spreads over a base of area pi(5^2) = 25*pi square inches. The new depth is 40*pi divided by 25*pi, which equals 1.6 inches, comfortably below the 15 inch height of the container.
questions.trap: Students scale the depth by the ratio of the radii and compute 10 x (2/5) = 4. Base area grows with the square of the radius, so the correct scaling factor is (2/5)^2 = 4/25, which gives 1.6 rather than 4.

questions.question: A closed box is a rectangular solid whose width, height and length are in the ratio 1 to 2 to 3. The volume of the box is 750 cubic inches. What is the total surface area of the closed box, in square inches?
questions.explanation: Write the three dimensions as x, 2x and 3x. Their product is 6*x^3, so 6*x^3 = 750 and x^3 = 125, giving x = 5. The box therefore measures 5 by 10 by 15. Its surface area is 2(5 x 10 + 10 x 15 + 15 x 5) = 2(50 + 150 + 75) = 2(275) = 550 square inches.
questions.trap: Students find x = 5 and then report a single face area, or they forget the factor of 2 that accounts for opposite faces and answer 275. A closed box has three pairs of congruent faces, so the sum of the three distinct face areas must be doubled.

questions.question: A shipping crate is a rectangular box measuring 24 inches by 18 inches by 16 inches. The crate and its contents together have a mass of 84 kilograms. Density is the ratio of mass to volume, and 1 foot equals 12 inches. What is the density of the loaded crate, in kilograms per cubic foot?
questions.explanation: The crate's volume is 24 x 18 x 16 = 6,912 cubic inches. Since 1 foot is 12 inches, one cubic foot is 12^3 = 1,728 cubic inches, so the crate occupies 6,912/1,728 = 4 cubic feet. Density is mass divided by volume, giving 84/4 = 21 kilograms per cubic foot.
questions.trap: Students convert with a single factor of 12 instead of cubing it, dividing 6,912 by 12 to get 576 and arriving at a density near 0.15. Converting a volume requires the conversion factor to be applied once for each of the three dimensions, so 12^3 is the right divisor.

questions.question:
In the figure, A is the center of the circle and points B and D lie on the circle. Angle BAC is a right angle, C lies on ray AD beyond D, and DC is one-third the length of AD. The radius of the circle is 3m, where m is positive. Which of the following statements are true?

Indicate all such statements.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 240" width="320" height="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M130 140 L130 70 A70 70 0 0 1 200 140 Z" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"/><circle cx="130" cy="140" r="70" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="130" y1="140" x2="130" y2="70" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="130" y1="140" x2="223" y2="140" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="130" y1="70" x2="223" y2="140" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="130,130 140,130 140,140" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="130" cy="140" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><circle cx="200" cy="140" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><circle cx="130" cy="70" r="3" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="112" y="158" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">A</text><text x="122" y="62" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">B</text><text x="204" y="172" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">D</text><text x="226" y="158" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">C</text><text x="106" y="108" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">3m</text></svg>
options: A. The area of triangle ABC is 6*m^2.
B. The area of the sector bounded by radii AB and AD and the minor arc BD is 9*pi*m^2/4.
C. The area of that sector is greater than the area of triangle ABC.
D. The area of that sector is 9*pi*m^2.
E. The area of triangle ABC is greater than the area of that sector.
questions.explanation: Since AB and AD are radii, each has length 3m, and DC is one third of AD, so DC = m and AC = AD + DC = 4m. Triangle ABC has legs AB = 3m and AC = 4m meeting at the right angle at A, so its area is (1/2)(3m)(4m) = 6*m^2, which makes statement A true. The sector is a quarter of the circle because angle BAD is the same right angle, so its area is (1/4)(pi)(3m)^2 = 9*pi*m^2/4, which is about 7.07*m^2. That makes B true and D false. Comparing 7.07*m^2 with 6*m^2 shows the sector is the larger region, so C is true and E is false.
questions.trap: Students take the sector to be the whole circle and report 9*pi*m^2, or they treat AC as equal to AD and compute the triangle's area as 4.5*m^2, which would make the comparison look lopsided. The right angle at A makes the sector exactly one quarter of the circle, and C sits a third of a radius beyond D, so AC is four thirds of a radius.

questions.question:
Circle C and square S have the same perimeter. Which of the following statements must be true?

Indicate all such statements.
options: A. The area enclosed by C is greater than the area enclosed by S.
B. The ratio of the area enclosed by C to the area enclosed by S is 4/pi.
C. The area enclosed by C is more than 25 percent greater than the area enclosed by S.
D. The area enclosed by C is exactly twice the area enclosed by S.
E. The two enclosed areas are equal.
F. The ratio of the area enclosed by C to the area enclosed by S is pi/4.
questions.explanation: Call the common perimeter p. For the circle, 2*pi*r = p gives r = p/(2*pi), so its area is pi*r^2 = p^2/(4*pi). For the square, the side is p/4, so its area is p^2/16. Dividing, the ratio of circle area to square area is 16/(4*pi) = 4/pi, which is about 1.273. That makes B true and F false, since pi/4 is the reciprocal and is less than 1. A ratio above 1 makes A true, and 1.273 means the circle encloses about 27.3 percent more area, so C is true while D and E are false.
questions.trap: Students reach for pi/4, the familiar ratio of a circle's area to the area of the square that circumscribes it, and endorse F. That ratio applies when the square's side equals the circle's diameter, not when the two figures share a perimeter; with equal perimeters the circle is the larger region, so the ratio must exceed 1.
